entries.eefb8e18ab9bf00f9fe7bc02806c5ad59c8c8c4c: <div sID="gen1947" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Exod.25" sID="Exod.25"/> <div eID="gen1947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1948" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1949" type="x-p"/> At this chapter begins an account of the orders and instructions God gave to Moses upon the mount for the erecting and furnishing of a tabernacle to the honour of God. We have here. I. Orders given for a collection to be made among the people for this purpose, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.1-Exod.25.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. Particular instructions, 1. Concerning the ark of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.10-Exod.25.22">ver. 10-22</reference>. 2. The table of showbread, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.23-Exod.25.30">ver. 23-30</reference>. 3. The golden candlestick, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.31-Exod.25.40">ver. 31</reference>, &c.
entries.382529e3e6958ce9f45a44b5227f44cd115a4760: <div eID="gen1949" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1948" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Tabernacle and Its Furniture. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring me an offering: of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering. <hi type="super">3</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the offering which ye shall take of them; gold, and silver, and brass, <hi type="super">4</hi> And blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine linen, and goats' <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood, <hi type="super">6</hi> Oil for the light, spices for anointing oil, and for sweet incense, <hi type="super">7</hi> Onyx stones, and stones to be set in the ephod, and in the breastplate. <hi type="super">8</hi> And let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them. <hi type="super">9</hi> According to all that I show thee, <hi type="italic">after</hi> the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen1950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1951" type="x-p"/> We may suppose that when Moses went into the midst of the cloud, and abode there so long, where the holy angels attended the <hi type="italic">shechinah,</hi> or divine Majesty, he saw and heard very glorious things relating to the upper world, but they were things which it was not lawful nor possible to utter; and therefore, in the records he kept of the transactions there, he says nothing to satisfy the curiosity of those who would intrude into the things which they have not seen, but writes that only which he was to speak to the children of Israel. For the scripture is designed to direct us in our duty, not to fill our heads with speculations, nor to please our fancies. <div eID="gen1951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1952" type="x-p"/> In these verses God tells Moses his intention in general, that the children of Israel should build him a sanctuary, for he designed to <hi type="italic">dwell among them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.8">v. 8</reference>); and some think that, though there were altars and groves used for religious worship before this, yet there never was any house, or temple, built for sacred uses in any nation before this tabernacle was erected by Moses, and that all the temples which were afterwards so much celebrated among the heathen took rise from this and pattern by it. God had chosen the people of Israel to be a peculiar people to himself (above all people), among whom divine revelation, and a religion according to it, should be lodged and established: he himself would be their King. As their King, he had already given them laws for the government of themselves, and their dealings one with another, with some general rules for religious worship, according to the light of reason and the law of nature, in the ten commandments and the following comments upon them. But this was not thought sufficient to distinguish them from other nations, or to answer to the extent of that covenant which God would make with them to be <hi type="italic">their God;</hi> and therefore, <div eID="gen1952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1953" type="x-p"/> I. He orders a royal palace to be set up among them for himself, here called <hi type="italic">a sanctuary,</hi> or <hi type="italic">holy place,</hi> or <hi type="italic">habitation,</hi> of which it is said (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer. xvii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary.</hi> This sanctuary is to be considered, <div eID="gen1953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1954" type="x-p"/> 1. As ceremonial, consonant to the other institutions of that dispensation, which consisted in carnal ordinances (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>); hence it is called a <hi type="italic">worldly sanctuary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">Heb. ix. 1</reference>. God in it kept his court, as Israel's King. (1.) There he manifested his presence among them, and it was intended for a sign or token of his presence, that, while they had that in the midst of them, they might never again ask, <hi type="italic">Is the Lord among us or not?</hi> And, because in the wilderness they dwelt in tents, even this royal palace was ordered to be a tabernacle too, that it might move with them, and might be an instance of the condescension of the divine favour. (2.) There he ordered his subjects to attend him with their homage and tribute. Thither they must come to consult his oracles, thither they must bring their sacrifices, and there all Israel must meet, to pay their joint respects to the God of Israel. <div eID="gen1954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1955" type="x-p"/> 2. As typical; the holy places made with hands were the <hi type="italic">figures of the true,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>. The gospel church is the true <hi type="italic">tabernacle, which the Lord hath pitched, and not man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">Heb. viii. 2</reference>. The body of Christ, in and by which he made atonement, was the <hi type="italic">greater and more perfect tabernacle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">Heb. ix. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us,</hi> as in a tabernacle. <div eID="gen1955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1956" type="x-p"/> II. When Moses was to erect this palace, it was requisite that he should first be instructed where he must have the materials, and where he must have the model; for he could neither contrive it by his own ingenuity nor build it at his own charge; he is therefore directed here concerning both. <div eID="gen1956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1957" type="x-p"/> 1. The people must furnish him with the materials, not by a tax imposed upon them, but by a voluntary contribution. This is the first thing concerning which orders are here given. <div eID="gen1957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1958" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Speak unto the children of Israel that they bring me an offering;</hi> and there was all the reason in the world that they should, for (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.1">v. 1</reference>), [1.] It was God himself that had not only enlarged them, but enriched them with the spoils of the Egyptians. He had instructed them to borrow, and he had inclined the Egyptians to lend, so that from him they had their wealth, and therefore it was fit they should devote it to him and use it for him, and thus make a grateful acknowledgement of the favours they had received. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The best use we can make of our worldly wealth is to honour God with it in works of piety and charity. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> When we have been blessed with some remarkable success in our affairs, and have had, as we say, a good turn, it may be justly expected that we should do something more than ordinary for the glory of God, consecrating our gain, in some reasonable proportion of it, to the Lord of the whole earth, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.3">Mic. iv. 13</reference>. [2.] The sanctuary that was to be built was intended for their benefit and comfort, and therefore they must be at the expense of it. They had been unworthy of the privilege if they had grudged at the charge. They might well afford to offer liberally for the honour of God, while they lived at free quarters, having food for themselves and their families rained upon them daily from heaven. We also must own that we have our all from God's bounty, and therefore ought to use all for his glory. Since we live upon him, we must live to him. <div eID="gen1958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1959" type="x-p"/> (2.) This offering must be given willingly, and with the heart, that is, [1.] It was not prescribed to them what or how much they must give, but it was left to their generosity, that they might show their good-will to the house of God and the offices thereof, and might do it with a holy emulation, the zeal of a few <hi type="italic">provoking many,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2 Cor. ix. 2</reference>. We should ask, not only, "What must we do?" but, "What may we do for God?" [2.] Whatever they gave, they must give it cheerfully, not grudgingly and with reluctance, for <hi type="italic">God loves a cheerful giver,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. What is laid out in the service of God we must reckon well bestowed. <div eID="gen1959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1960" type="x-p"/> (3.) The particulars are here mentioned which they must offer (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.3-Exod.25.7">v. 3-7</reference>), all of them things that there would be occasion for in the tabernacle, or the service of it. Some observe that here was gold, silver, and brass, provided, but no iron; that is the military metal, and this was to be a house of peace. Every thing that was provided was very rich and fine, and the best of the sort; for God, who is the best, should have the best. <div eID="gen1960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1961" type="x-p"/> 2. God himself would furnish him with the model: <hi type="italic">According to all that I show thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.25.9">v. 9</reference>. God showed him an exact plan of it, in miniature, which he must conform to in all points. Thus Ezekiel saw in vision the form of the house and the fashion thereof, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Ezek. xliii. 11</reference>. Note, Whatsoever is done in God's service must be done by his direction, and not otherwise. Yet God did not only show him the model, but gave him also particular directions how to frame the tabernacle according to that model, in all the parts of it, which he goes over distinctly in this and the following chapters. When Moses, in the beginning of Genesis, was to describe the creation of the world, though it is such a stately and curious fabric and made up of such a variety and vast number of particulars, yet he gave a very short and general account of it, and nothing compared with what the wisdom of this world would have desired and expected from one that wrote by divine revelation; but, when he comes to describe the tabernacle, he does it with the greatest niceness and accuracy imaginable. He that gave us no account of the lines and circles of the globe, the diameter of the earth, or the height and magnitude of the stars, has told us particularly the measure of every board and curtain of the tabernacle; for God's church and instituted religion are more precious to him and more considerable than all the rest of the world. And the scriptures were written, not to describe to us the works of nature, a general view of which is sufficient to lead us to the knowledge and service of the Creator, but to acquaint us with the methods of grace, and those things which are purely matters of divine revelation. The blessedness of the future state is more fully represented under the notion of a new Jerusalem than under the notion of new heavens and a new earth.
entries.03c468a36a2ebd1f647a269a3b625204d6877b93: <div eID="gen1961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1962" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And they shall make an ark <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood: two cubits and a half <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof. <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, within and without shalt thou overlay it, and shalt make upon it a crown of gold round about. <hi type="super">12</hi> And thou shalt cast four rings of gold for it, and put <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the four corners thereof; and two rings <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in the one side of it, and two rings in the other side of it. <hi type="super">13</hi> And thou shalt make staves <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood, and overlay them with gold. <hi type="super">14</hi> And thou shalt put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark, that the ark may be borne with them. <hi type="super">15</hi> The staves shall be in the rings of the ark: they shall not be taken from it. <hi type="super">16</hi> And thou shalt put into the ark the testimony which I shall give thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> And thou shalt make a mercy seat <hi type="italic">of</hi> pure gold: two cubits and a half <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof. <hi type="super">18</hi> And thou shalt make two cherubims <hi type="italic">of</hi> gold, <hi type="italic">of</hi> beaten work shalt thou make them, in the two ends of the mercy seat. <hi type="super">19</hi> And make one cherub on the one end, and the other cherub on the other end: <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the mercy seat shall ye make the cherubims on the two ends thereof. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the cherubims shall stretch forth <hi type="italic">their</hi> wings on high, covering the mercy seat with their wings, and their faces <hi type="italic">shall look</hi> one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubims be. <hi type="super">21</hi> And thou shalt put the mercy seat above upon the ark; and in the ark thou shalt put the testimony that I shall give thee. <hi type="super">22</hi> And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the ark of the testimony, of all <hi type="italic">things</hi> which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel. <div eID="gen1962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1963" type="x-p"/> The first thing which is here ordered to be made is the ark with its appurtenances, the furniture of the most holy place, and the special token of God's presence, for which the tabernacle was erected to be the receptacle. <div eID="gen1963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1964" type="x-p"/> I. The ark itself was a chest, or coffer, in which the two tables of the law, written with the finger of God, were to be honourably deposited, and carefully kept. The dimensions of it are exactly ordered; if the Jewish cubit was, as some learned men compute, three inches longer than our half-yard (twenty-one inches in all), this chest or cabinet was about fifty-two inches long, thirty-one broad, and thirty-one deep. It was overlaid within and without with thin plates of gold. It had a crown, or cornice, of gold, round it, with rings and staves to carry it with; and in it he must put the testimony, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.10-Exod.25.16">v. 10-16</reference>. The tables of the law are called the <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> because God did in them testify his will: his giving them that law was in token of his favour to them; and their acceptance of it was in token of their subjection and obedience to him. This law was a testimony to them, to direct them in their duty, and would be a testimony against them if they transgressed. The ark is called the <hi type="italic">ark of the testimony</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.6">ch. xxx. 6</reference>), and the tabernacle <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of the testimony</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.10.11">Num. x. 11</reference>) or witness, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.44">Acts vii. 44</reference>. The gospel of Christ is also called a testimony or witness, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Matt. xxiv. 14</reference>. It is observable, 1. That the tables of the law were carefully preserved in the ark for the purpose, to teach us to make much of the word of God, and to hide it in our hearts, in our innermost thoughts, as the ark was placed in the holy of holies. It intimates likewise the care which divine Providence ever did, and ever will, take to preserve the records of divine revelation in the church, so that even in the latter days there shall be seen in his temple the <hi type="italic">ark of his testament.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rev.11.19">Rev. xi. 19</reference>. 2. That this ark was the chief token of God's presence, which teaches us that the first and great evidence and assurance of God's favour is the putting of his law in the heart. God dwells where that rules, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb. viii. 10</reference>. 3. That provision was made for the carrying of this ark about with them in all their removals, which intimates to us that, wherever we go, we should take our religion along with us, always bearing about with us the love of the Lord Jesus, and his law. <div eID="gen1964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1965" type="x-p"/> II. The mercy-seat was the covering of the ark or chest, made of solid gold, exactly to fit the dimensions of the ark, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.17">v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.21">21</reference>. This <hi type="italic">propitiatory covering,</hi> as it might well be translated, was a type of Christ, the great propitiation, whose satisfaction fully answers the demands of the law, covers our transgressions, and comes between us and the curse we deserve. Thus he is the <hi type="italic">end of the law for righteousness.</hi> <div eID="gen1965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1966" type="x-p"/> III. The cherubim of gold were fixed to the mercy-seat, and of a piece with it, and spread their wings over it, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.18">v. 18</reference>. It is supposed that these cherubim were designed to represent the holy angels, who always attended the <hi type="italic">shechinah,</hi> or divine Majesty, particularly at the giving of the law; not by any effigies of an angel, but some emblem of the angelical nature, probably some one of those four faces spoken of, <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.10">Ezek. i. 10</reference>. Whatever the faces were, they looked one towards another, and both downward towards the ark, while their wings were stretched out so as to touch one another. The apostle calls them <hi type="italic">cherubim of glory shadowing the mercy-seat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.5">Heb. ix. 5</reference>. It denotes their attendance upon the Redeemer, to whom they were ministering spirits, their readiness to do his will, their special presence in the assemblies of saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Ps. lxviii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1 Cor. xi. 10</reference>), and their desire to look into the mysteries of the gospel which they diligently contemplate, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1 Pet. i. 12</reference>. God is said to dwell, or sit, <hi type="italic">between the cherubim,</hi> on the mercy-seat (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Ps. lxxx. 1</reference>), and thence he here promises, for the future, to meet with Moses, and to <hi type="italic">commune with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">v. 22</reference>. There he would give law, and there he would give audience, as a prince on his throne; and thus he manifests himself willing to be reconciled to us, and keep up communion with us, in and by the mediation of Christ. In allusion to this mercy-seat, we are said to come boldly to <hi type="italic">the throne of grace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>); for we <hi type="italic">are not under the law,</hi> which is covered, <hi type="italic">but under grace,</hi> which is displayed; its wings are stretched out, and we are invited to come under the shadow of them, <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">Ruth ii. 12</reference>.
entries.3adf602dcc4c88a7307f33a11a1f0c4fe224545f: <div eID="gen1966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super"></hi> 23 Thou shalt also make a table <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood: two cubits <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof. <hi type="super">24</hi> And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, and make thereto a crown of gold round about. <hi type="super">25</hi> And thou shalt make unto it a border of an hand breadth round about, and thou shalt make a golden crown to the border thereof round about. <hi type="super">26</hi> And thou shalt make for it four rings of gold, and put the rings in the four corners that <hi type="italic">are</hi> on the four feet thereof. 27 Over against the border shall the rings be for places of the staves to bear the table. <hi type="super">28</hi> And thou shalt make the staves <hi type="italic">of</hi> shittim wood, and overlay them with gold, that the table may be borne with them. <hi type="super">29</hi> And thou shalt make the dishes thereof, and spoons thereof, and covers thereof, and bowls thereof, to cover withal: <hi type="italic">of</hi> pure gold shalt thou make them. 30 And thou shalt set upon the table showbread before me alway. <div eID="gen1967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1968" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A table ordered to be made of wood overlaid with gold, which was to stand, not in the holy of holies (nothing was in that but the ark with its appurtenances), but in the outer part of the tabernacle, called the <hi type="italic">sanctuary,</hi> or <hi type="italic">holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.2">Heb. ix. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">23</reference>, &c. There must also be the usual furniture of the sideboard, dishes and spoons, &c., and all <hi type="italic">of gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.25.29">v. 29</reference>. 2. This table was to be always spread, and furnished with the show-bread (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.30">v. 30</reference>), or <hi type="italic">bread of faces,</hi> twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set in two rows, six in a row; see the law concerning them, <reference osisRef="Lev.24.5-Lev.24.10">Lev. xxiv. 5</reference>, &c. The tabernacle being God's house, in which he was pleased to say that he would dwell among them, he would show that he kept a good house. In the royal palace it was fit that there should be a royal table. Some make the twelve loaves to represent the twelve tribes, set before God as his people and <hi type="italic">the corn of his floor,</hi> as they are called, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. As the ark signified God's being present with them, so the twelve loaves signified their being presented to God. This bread was designed to be, (1.) A thankful acknowledgement of God's goodness to them, in giving them their daily bread, manna in the wilderness, where he prepared a table for them, and, in Canaan, the corn of the land. Hereby they owned their dependence upon Providence, not only for the corn in the field, which they gave thanks for in offering the sheaf of first-fruits, but for the bread in their houses, that, when it was brought home, God did not <hi type="italic">blow upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. i. 9</reference>. Christ has taught us to pray every day for the bread of the day. (2.) A token of their communion with God. This bread on God's table being made of the same corn with the bread on their own tables, God and Israel did, as it were, eat together, as a pledge of friendship and fellowship; he supped with them, and they with him. (3.) A type of the spiritual provision which is made in the church, by the gospel of Christ, for all that are made priests to our God. <hi type="italic">In our Father's house there is bread enough and to spare,</hi> a loaf for every tribe. All that attend in God's house shall be abundantly satisfied with the goodness of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Ps. xxxvi. 8</reference>. Divine consolations are the continual feast of holy souls, notwithstanding there are those to whom <hi type="italic">the table of the Lord,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">meat thereof</hi> (because it is plain bread), are <hi type="italic">contemptible,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.12">Mal. i. 12</reference>. Christ has a table in his kingdom, at which all his saints shall for every eat and drink with him, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Luke xxii. 30</reference>.
entries.3b67d64ea11049d67d6676ce06debbd7bd2c8ef1: <div eID="gen1968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And thou shalt make a candlestick <hi type="italic">of</hi> pure gold: <hi type="italic">of</hi> beaten work shall the candlestick be made: his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same. <hi type="super">32</hi> And six branches shall come out of the sides of it; three branches of the candlestick out of the one side, and three branches of the candlestick out of the other side: 33 Three bowls made like unto almonds, <hi type="italic">with</hi> a knop and a flower in one branch; and three bowls made like almonds in the other branch, <hi type="italic">with</hi> a knop and a flower: so in the six branches that come out of the candlestick. <hi type="super">34</hi> And in the candlestick <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> four bowls made like unto almonds, <hi type="italic">with</hi> their knops and their flowers. <hi type="super">35</hi> And <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> a knop under two branches of the same, and a knop under two branches of the same, and a knop under two branches of the same, according to the six branches that proceed out of the candlestick. <hi type="super">36</hi> Their knops and their branches shall be of the same: all it <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> one beaten work <hi type="italic">of</hi> pure gold. <hi type="super">37</hi> And thou shalt make the seven lamps thereof: and they shall light the lamps thereof, that they may give light over against it. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, <hi type="italic">shall be of</hi> pure gold. <hi type="super">39</hi> <hi type="italic">Of</hi> a talent of pure gold shall he make it, with all these vessels. <hi type="super">40</hi> And look that thou make <hi type="italic">them</hi> after their pattern, which was showed thee in the mount. <div eID="gen1969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1970" type="x-p"/> I. The next thing ordered to be made for the furnishing of God's palace was a rich stately candlestick, all of pure gold, not hollow, but solid. The particular directions here given concerning it show, 1. That it was very magnificent, and a great ornament to the place; it had many branches drawn from the main shaft, which had not only their bowls (to put the oil and the kindled wick in) for necessity, but knops and flowers for ornament. 2. That it was very convenient, and admirably contrived both to scatter the light and to keep the tabernacle clean from smoke and snuffs. 3. That it was very significant. The tabernacle had no windows by which to let in the light of the day, all its light was candle-light, which intimates the comparative darkness of that dispensation, while the Sun or righteousness had not as yet risen, nor had the day-star from on high yet visited his church. Yet God left not himself without witness, nor them without instruction; the commandment was a lamp, and the law a light, and the prophets were branches from that lamp, which gave light in their several ages to the Old-Testament church. The church is still dark, as the tabernacle was, in comparison with what it will be in heaven; but the word of God is the candlestick, <hi type="italic">a light shining in a dark place</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2 Pet. i. 19</reference>), and a dark place indeed the world would be without it. The Spirit of God, in his various gifts and graces, is compared to the <hi type="italic">seven lamps</hi> which <hi type="italic">burn before the throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">Rev. iv. 5</reference>. The churches are golden candlesticks, the lights of the world, <hi type="italic">holding forth the word of life</hi> as the candlestick does the light, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15-Phil.2.16">Phil. ii. 15, 16</reference>. Ministers are to light the lamps, and snuff them (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.37">v. 37</reference>), by opening the scriptures. The treasure of this light is now put into <hi type="italic">earthen vessels,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6-2Cor.4.7">2 Cor. iv. 6, 7</reference>. The branches of the candlestick spread every way, to denote the diffusing of the light of the gospel into all parts by the Christian ministry, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14-Matt.5.15">Matt. v. 14, 15</reference>. There is a <hi type="italic">diversity of gifts,</hi> but the same Spirit gives to each to profit withal. <div eID="gen1970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1971" type="x-p"/> II. There is in the midst of these instructions an express caution given to Moses, to take heed of varying from his model: <hi type="italic">Make them after the pattern shown thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.25.40">v. 40</reference>. Nothing was left to his own invention, or the fancy of the workmen, or the people's humour; but the will of God must be religiously observed in every particular. Thus, 1. All God's providences are exactly according to his counsels, and the copy never varies from the original. Infinite Wisdom never changes its measures; whatever is purposed shall undoubtedly be performed. 2. All his ordinances must be administered according to his institutions. Christ's instruction to his disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>) is similar to this: <hi type="italic">Observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.</hi>  <chapter eID="Exod.25"/> <div eID="gen1971" type="x-p"/>

entries.d0c907f76004257995b39e3139f85e4ec53c7a01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv830"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.25.1-Exod.25.40">Ex 25:1-40</reference>. Concerning an Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv830"/><hi type="bold">1. the Lord spake unto Moses, &c.--</hi>The business that chiefly occupied Moses on the mount, whatever other disclosures were made to him there, was in receiving directions about the tabernacle, and they are here recorded as given to him. <div eID="gen1159" type="x-p"/>
entries.34ffc9878a4576af096e095c94928e08703bad25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv831"/><div sID="gen1160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv831"/><hi type="bold">2. bring me an offering of every man that giveth it willingly, &c.--</hi>Having declared allegiance to God as their sovereign, they were expected to contribute to His state, as other subjects to their kings; and the "offering" required of them was not to be imposed as a tax, but to come from their own loyal and liberal feelings. <div eID="gen1160" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e67f232373c82eb88dfaff37117b01997506df0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv832"/><div sID="gen1161" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv832"/><hi type="bold">3. this is the offering which ye shall take of them--</hi>the articles of which the offerings should consist.<div eID="gen1161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brass--</hi>rather copper, brass being a composite metal. <div eID="gen1162" type="x-p"/>
entries.02ffa9571e2eef5880417bafdb11056bb938e686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv833"/><div sID="gen1163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv833"/><hi type="bold">4. goats' hair--</hi>or leather of goats' skin. <div eID="gen1163" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b13b40c8e9fa2346ff1383fbad0700e9777bc46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv834"/><div sID="gen1164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv834"/><hi type="bold">5. badgers' skins--</hi>The badger was an unclean animal, and is not a native of the East--rather some kind of fish, of the leather of which sandals are made in the East. [See on <reference osisRef="Exod.39.34">Ex 39:34</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.10">Eze 16:10</reference>.]<div eID="gen1164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shittim wood--</hi>or Shittah (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Is 41:19</reference>), the acacia, a shrub which grows plentifully in the deserts of Arabia, yielding a light, strong, and beautiful wood, in long planks. <div eID="gen1165" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0523c255c27dc7b106590114b692cc8a6dbad3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv835"/><div sID="gen1166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv835"/><hi type="bold">7. ephod--</hi>a square cloak, hanging down from the shoulders, and worn by priests. <div eID="gen1166" type="x-p"/>
entries.34e7afc2c57448711d84a0acdbf860e7e4c91347: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv836"/><div sID="gen1167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv836"/><hi type="bold">8. a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them--</hi>In one sense the tabernacle was to be a palace, the royal residence of the King of Israel, in which He was to dwell among His people, receive their petitions, and issue His responses. But it was also to be a place of worship, in which God was to record His name and to enshrine the mystic symbols of His presence. <div eID="gen1167" type="x-p"/>
entries.03c851f61759d20a0ad5e6f43c75e767326decd2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv837"/><div sID="gen1168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv837"/><hi type="bold">9. According to all that I show thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle--</hi>The proposed erection could be, in the circumstances of the Israelites, not of a fixed and stable but of a temporary and movable description, capable of being carried about with them in their various sojournings. It was made after "the pattern" shown to Moses, by which is now generally understood, not that it was an unheard-of novelty, or an entirely original structure, for it is ascertained to have borne resemblance in form and arrangements to the style of an Egyptian temple, but that it was so altered, modified, and purified from all idolatrous associations, as to be appropriated to right objects, and suggestive of ideas connected with the true God and His worship. <div eID="gen1168" type="x-p"/>
entries.9df07adb8cada63702813458f1e8f932d68baba3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv838"/><div sID="gen1169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv838"/><hi type="bold">10. an ark--</hi>a coffer or chest, overlaid with gold, the dimensions of which, taking the cubit at eighteen inches, are computed to be three feet nine inches in length, two feet three inches in breadth. <div eID="gen1169" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fccc53bb62a9cf8bb9c0af58d780635c1d1a556: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv839"/><div sID="gen1170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv839"/><hi type="bold">11. a crown--</hi>a rim or cornice. <div eID="gen1170" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9b7373d379993d409fc8394d483fcbe0376154f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv840"/><div sID="gen1171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv840"/><hi type="bold">12. rings--</hi>staples for the poles, with which it was to be carried from place to place. <div eID="gen1171" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8cf4b31602f66c69a3c5f002cda363d6c475ee0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv841"/><div sID="gen1172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv841"/><hi type="bold">15. staves shall be in the rings of the ark--</hi>that is, always remain in the rings, whether the ark be at rest or in motion. <div eID="gen1172" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc88c86fa862a551841a99daa1767e67aa7f3736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv842"/><div sID="gen1173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv842"/><hi type="bold">16. the testimony--</hi>that is, the two tables of stone, containing the ten commandments, and called "the testimony," because by it God did testify His sovereign authority over Israel as His people, His selection of them as the guardians of His will and worship, and His displeasure in the event of their transgressing His laws; while on their part, by receiving and depositing this law in its appointed place, they testified their acknowledgment of God's right to rule over them, and their submission to the authority of His law. The superb and elaborate style of the ark that contained "the testimony" was emblematic of the great treasure it held; in other words, the incomparable value and excellence of the Word of God, while its being placed in this chest further showed the great care which God has ever taken for preserving it. <div eID="gen1173" type="x-p"/>
entries.08c3aac3aeea4cc016e443ecbe5ad97e3790dbff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv843"/><div sID="gen1174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv843"/><hi type="bold">17. thou shalt make a mercy seat of pure gold--</hi>to serve as a lid, covering it exactly. It was "the propitiatory cover," as the term may be rendered, denoting that Christ, our great propitiation [1Jo 2:2; 4:10], has fully answered all the demands of the law, covers our transgressions, and comes between us and the curse of a violated law. <div eID="gen1174" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f353c3a9aee9a134010dff7d01b4a12ed4a4990: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv844"/><div sID="gen1175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv844"/><hi type="bold">18. two cherubim--</hi>The real meaning of these figures, as well as the shape or form of them, is not known with certainty--probably similar to what was afterwards introduced into the temple, and described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.8-Ezek.10.22">Eze 10:8-22</reference>. They stretched out their wings, and their faces were turned towards the mercy seat [Ex 25:20], probably in a bowing attitude. The prevailing opinion now is, that those splendid figures were symbolical not of angelic but of earthly and human beings--the members of the Church of God interested in the dispensation of grace, the redeemed in every age--and that these hieroglyphic forms symbolized the qualities of the true people of God--courage, patience, intelligence, and activity. <div eID="gen1175" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e3041e1f944d7c83fb551a001ed95a8e940386e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv845"/><div sID="gen1176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv845"/><hi type="bold">22. there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat--</hi>The Shekinah, or symbol of the Divine Presence, rested on the mercy seat, and was indicated by a cloud, from the midst of which responses were audibly given when God was consulted on behalf of His people. Hence God is described as "dwelling" or "sitting" between the cherubim. <div eID="gen1176" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4486be1c6b1a999e98ed1ae026a3811d5f0ec40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv846"/><div sID="gen1177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv846"/><hi type="bold">23. table of shittim wood--</hi>of the same material and decorations as the ark [see on Ex 25:5], and like it, too, furnished with rings for the poles on which it was carried [Ex 25:26]. The staves, however, were taken out of it when stationary, in order not to encumber the priests while engaged in their services at the table. It was half a cubit less than the ark in length and breadth, but of the same height. [See on <reference osisRef="Exod.25.10">Ex 25:10</reference>.] <div eID="gen1177" type="x-p"/>
entries.a38ffe08858c7b4034082e56f2baff65bac426c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv847"/><div sID="gen1178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv847"/><hi type="bold">24. crown--</hi>the moulding or ornamental rim, which is thought to have been raised above the level of the table, to prevent anything from falling off. <div eID="gen1178" type="x-p"/>
entries.d30ca3c96675c5341132056ad4bc3f66f5e13808: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv848"/><div sID="gen1179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv848"/><hi type="bold">29. dishes--</hi>broad platters.<div eID="gen1179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spoons--</hi>cups or concave vessels, used for holding incense.<div eID="gen1180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covers--</hi>both for bread and incense.<div eID="gen1181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowls--</hi>cups; for though no mention is made of wine, libations were undoubtedly made to God, according to Josephus and the rabbins, once a week, when the bread was changed.<div eID="gen1182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to cover withal--</hi>rather, "to pour out withal." <div eID="gen1183" type="x-p"/>
entries.fddec827bc2e232947c825c8c51192ecfcf202f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv849"/><div sID="gen1184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv849"/><hi type="bold">30. showbread--</hi>literally, presence bread, so called because it was constantly exhibited before the Lord, or because the bread of His presence, like the angel of His presence, pointed symbolically to Christ. It consisted of twelve unleavened loaves, said traditionally to have been laid in piles of six each. This bread was designed to be a symbol of the full and never-failing provision which is made in the Church for the spiritual sustenance and refreshment of God's people. <div eID="gen1184" type="x-p"/>
entries.96aefcc0b6d8068cff57dccb6f3dd6166a7f614f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv850"/><div sID="gen1185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv850"/><hi type="bold">31. candlestick--</hi>literally, "a lamp bearer." It was so constructed as to be capable of being taken to pieces for facility in removal. The shaft or stock rested on a pedestal. It had seven branches, shaped like reeds or canes--three on each side, with one in the center--and worked out into knobs, flowers, and bowls, placed alternately [Ex 25:32-36]. The figure represented on the arch of Titus gives the best idea of this candlestick. <div eID="gen1185" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d0f7908079698ca258845ba503e8c4468b791e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv851"/><div sID="gen1186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv851"/><hi type="bold">33. knops--</hi>old spelling for "knobs"--bosses. <div eID="gen1186" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa9bdc9945d2ba202685a392c51d269b3b6be886: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv852"/><div sID="gen1187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv852"/><hi type="bold">37. they shall light the lamps ... that they may give light--</hi>The light was derived from pure olive oil, and probably kept continually burning (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.30.7">Ex 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.24.2">Le 24:2</reference>). <div eID="gen1187" type="x-p"/>
entries.102e489c6b03fac325df9e2bd387eb121be6237f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv853"/><div sID="gen1188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv853"/><hi type="bold">38. tongs--</hi>snuffers. <div eID="gen1188" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bc942400f7ee35cbef9d9b741fc7e0f850db30a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv854"/><div sID="gen1189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv854"/><hi type="bold">39. a talent of pure gold--</hi>in weight equivalent to 125 lbs. troy. <div eID="gen1189" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b3c07502fccb2007ae708f6f59f9af83ee3afcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv855"/><div sID="gen1190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv855"/><hi type="bold">40. look that thou make them after their pattern--</hi>This caution, which is repeated with no small frequency in other parts of the narrative, is an evidence of the deep interest taken by the Divine King in the erection of His palace or sanctuary; and it is impossible to account for the circumstance of God's condescending to such minute details, except on the assumption that this tabernacle was to be of a typical character, and eminently subservient to the religious instruction and benefit of mankind, by shadowing forth in its leading features the grand truths of the Christian Church. <chapter eID="Exod.25"/>

entries.4f63eea66f95e6327f82bf6b1d761add951cffa1: <div eID="gen3568" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen3569" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3570" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3570" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3569" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3571" type="x-p"/> The Lord addresses Moses out of the Divine glory, and commands him to speak unto the Israelites, that they may give him free-will offerings, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.1">Exo 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.2">Exo 25:2</reference>. The different kinds of offerings, gold, silver, and brass, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.3">Exo 25:3</reference>. Purple, scarlet, fine linen, and goats' hair, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.4">Exo 25:4</reference>. Rams' skins, badgers' skins, (rather violet-coloured skins), and shittim wood, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.5">Exo 25:5</reference>. Oil and spices, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.6">Exo 25:6</reference>. Onyx stones, and stones for the ephod and breastplate, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.7">Exo 25:7</reference>. A sanctuary is to be made after the pattern of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.8">Exo 25:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.9">Exo 25:9</reference>. The ark and its dimensions, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.10">Exo 25:10</reference>. Its crown of gold, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.11">Exo 25:11</reference>. Its rings, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.12">Exo 25:12</reference>. Its staves, and their use, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.13-Exo.25.15">Exo 25:13-15</reference>. The testimony to be laid up in the ark, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.16">Exo 25:16</reference>. The mercy-seat and its dimensions, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.17">Exo 25:17</reference>. The cherubim, how made and placed, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.18-Exo.25.20">Exo 25:18-20</reference>. The mercy-seat to be placed on the ark, and the testimony to be put within it, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.21">Exo 25:21</reference>. The Lord promises to commune with the people from the mercy-seat, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>. The table of shew-bread, and its dimensions, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.23">Exo 25:23</reference>. Its crown and border of gold, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.24">Exo 25:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.25">Exo 25:25</reference>. Its rings, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.26">Exo 25:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.27">Exo 25:27</reference>. Staves, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.28">Exo 25:28</reference>. Dishes, spoons, and bowls, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.29">Exo 25:29</reference>. Its use, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.30">Exo 25:30</reference>. The golden candlestick; its branches, bowls, knops, and flowers, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.31-Exo.25.36">Exo 25:31-36</reference>. Its seven lamps, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.37">Exo 25:37</reference>. Tongs and snuffers, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.38">Exo 25:38</reference>. The weight of the candlestick and its utensils, one talent of gold, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.39">Exo 25:39</reference>. All to be made according to the pattern showed to Moses on the mount, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.40">Exo 25:40</reference>.
entries.9a999afb5d851143f09c06775843b29150fd99ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen3571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3572" type="x-p"/> That they bring me an offering - The offering here mentioned is the תרומה terumah, a kind of free-will offering, consisting of any thing that was necessary for the occasion. It signifies properly any thing that was lifted up, the heave-offering, because in presenting it to God it was lifted up to be laid on his altar; but see Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference> (note). God requires that they should build him a tent, suited in some sort to his dignity and eminence, because he was to act as their king, and to dwell among them; and they were to consider themselves as his subjects, and in this character to bring him presents, which was considered to be the duty of every subject appearing before his prince. See <reference osisRef="Exo.23.15">Exo 23:15</reference>.
entries.bef20801a766eebd49e6e2ef2498de36085bcb8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen3572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3573" type="x-p"/> This is the offering - There were three kinds of metals: <div eID="gen3573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> 1. Gold, זהב zahab, which may properly signify wrought gold; what was bright and resplendent, as the word implies. In <reference osisRef="Job.28.15">Job 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.19">Job 28:19</reference>, gold is mentioned five times, and four of the words are different in the original. <div eID="gen3574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3575" type="x-p"/> 1. סגור Segor, from סגר sagar, to shut up; gold in the mine, or shut up in its ore. <div eID="gen3575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3576" type="x-p"/> 2. כתם Kethem, from כתם catham, to sign, seal, or stamp; gold made current by being coined; standard or sterling gold, exhibiting the stamp expressive of its value. <div eID="gen3576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3577" type="x-p"/> 3. זהב Zahab, wrought gold, pure, highly polished gold; probably what was used for overlaying or gilding. <div eID="gen3577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3578" type="x-p"/> 4. פז Paz, denoting solidity, compactness, and strength; probably gold formed into different kinds of plate, as it is joined in <reference osisRef="Exo.25.17">Exo 25:17</reference> of the above chapter with כלי keley, vessels. The zahab, or pure gold, is here mentioned, because it was in a state that rendered it capable of being variously manufactured for the service of the sanctuary. <div eID="gen3578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3579" type="x-p"/> 2. Silver, כסף keseph, from casaph, to be pale, wan, or white; so called from its well-known color. <div eID="gen3579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3580" type="x-p"/> 3. Brass, נחשת nechosheth, copper; unless we suppose that the factitious metal commonly called brass is intended: this is formed by a combination of the oxide or ore of zinc, called lapis calaminaris, with copper. Brass seems to have been very anciently in use, as we find it mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.4.22">Gen 4:22</reference>; and the preparation of copper, to transform it into this factitious metal, seems to be very pointedly referred to <reference osisRef="Job.28.2">Job 28:2</reference> : Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone; אבן יצוק נחושה eben yatsuk nechushah, translated by the Vulgate, Lapis, solutus calore, in aes vertitur, "The stone, liquefied by heat, is turned into brass." Is it going too far to say that the stone here may refer to the lapis calaminaris, which was used to turn the copper into brass? Because brass was capable of so fine a polish as to become exceedingly bright, and keep its lustre a considerable time, hence it was used for all weapons of war and defensive armor among ancient nations; and copper seems to have been in no repute, but for its use in making brass.
entries.c842dc48e384d7db115112e7ac4bbc9e1d59829f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen3580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3581" type="x-p"/> Blue - תכלת techeleth, generally supposed to mean an azure or sky color; rendered by the Septuagint ὑακινθον, and by the Vulgate hyacinthum, a sky-blue or deep violet. <div eID="gen3581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3582" type="x-p"/> Purple - ארגמן argaman, a very precious color, extracted from the purpura or murex, a species of shell-fish, from which it is supposed the famous Tyrian purple came, so costly, and so much celebrated in antiquity. See this largely described, and the manner of dyeing it, in Pliny, Hist. Nat., lib. ix., c. 60-65, edit. Bipont. <div eID="gen3582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3583" type="x-p"/> Scarlet - תולעת tolaath, signifies a worm, of which this colouring matter was made; and, joined with שני shani, which signifies to repeat or double, implies that to strike this color the wool or cloth was twice dipped: hence the Vulgate renders the original coccum bis tinctum, "scarlet twice dyed;" and to this Horace refers, Odar., lib. ii., od. 16, v. 35: - Te Bis Afro Murice <div eID="gen3583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3584" type="x-p"/> Tinctae Vestiunt Lanae - "Thy robes the twice dyed purple stains." <div eID="gen3584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3585" type="x-p"/> It is the same color which the Arabs call al kermez, whence the French cramoisi, and the English crimson. On this subject much may be seen in Bochart, Calmet, and Scheuchzer. <div eID="gen3585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3586" type="x-p"/> Fine linen - שש shesh; whether this means linen, cotton, or silk, is not agreed on among interpreters. Because שש shesh signifies six, the rabbins suppose that it always signifies the fine linen of Egypt, in which six folds constituted one thread; and that when a single fold was meant, בד bad is the term used. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference>. <div eID="gen3586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3587" type="x-p"/> Goats' hair - עזים izzim, goats, but used here elliptically for goats' hair. In different parts of Asia Minor, Syria, Cilicia, and Phrygia, the goats have long, fine, and beautiful hair, in some cases almost as fine as silk, which they shear at proper times, and manufacture into garments. From Virgil, Georg. iii., v. 305-311, we learn that goats' hair manufactured into cloth was nearly of equal value with that formed from wool. <div eID="gen3587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3588" type="x-p"/> Hae quoque non cura nobis leviore tuendae <div eID="gen3588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3589" type="x-p"/> Nec minor usus erit: quamvis Milesia magno <div eID="gen3589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3590" type="x-p"/> Vellera mutentur, Tyrios incocta rubores. <div eID="gen3590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3591" type="x-p"/> Nec minus interea barbas incanaque menta <div eID="gen3591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3592" type="x-p"/> Cinyphii tondent hirci, setasque comantes, <div eID="gen3592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3593" type="x-p"/> Usum in castrorum, et miseris velamina nautis. "For hairy goats of equal profit are <div eID="gen3593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3594" type="x-p"/> With woolly sheep, and ask an equal care. 'Tis true the fleece when drunk with Tyrian juice <div eID="gen3594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3595" type="x-p"/> Is dearly sold, but not for needful use: <div eID="gen3595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3596" type="x-p"/> Meanwhile the pastor shears their hoary beards <div eID="gen3596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3597" type="x-p"/> And eases of their hair the loaden herds. <div eID="gen3597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3598" type="x-p"/> Their camelots, warm in tents, the soldier hold, <div eID="gen3598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3599" type="x-p"/> And shield the shivering mariner from the cold." <div eID="gen3599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3600" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.52714790258e63425435c6346e0bcdb7a1a71adb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen3600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3601" type="x-p"/> Rams' skins dyed red - ערת אילם מאדמים oroth eylim meoddamim, literally, the skins of red rams. It is a fact attested by many respectable travelers, that in the Levant sheep are often to be met with that have red or violet-coloured fleeces. And almost all ancient writers speak of the same thing. Homer describes the rams of Polyphemus as having a violet-coloured fleece. Αρσενες οΐες ησαν εΰτρεφεες, δασυμαλλοι, Καλοι τε, μεγαλοι τε, ιοδνεφες ειρος εχοντες. <div eID="gen3601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3602" type="x-p"/> Odyss., lib. ix., ver. 425. "Strong were the rams, with native purple fair, <div eID="gen3602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3603" type="x-p"/> Well fed, and largest of the fleecy care." <div eID="gen3603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3604" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen3604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3605" type="x-p"/> Pliny, Aristotle, and others mention the same. And from facts of this kind it is very probable that the fable of the golden fleece had its origin. In the Zetland Isles I have seen sheep with variously coloured fleeces, some white, some black, some black and white, some of a very fine chocolate color. Beholding those animals brought to my recollection those words of Virgil: - Ipse sed in pratis Aries jam suave rubenti <div eID="gen3605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3606" type="x-p"/> Murice, jam croceo mutabit vellera luto. <div eID="gen3606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3607" type="x-p"/> Eclog. iv., ver. 43. "No wool shall in dissembled colors shine; <div eID="gen3607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3608" type="x-p"/> But the luxurious father of the fold, <div eID="gen3608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3609" type="x-p"/> With native purple or unborrow'd gold, <div eID="gen3609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3610" type="x-p"/> Beneath his pompous fleece shall proudly sweat, <div eID="gen3610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3611" type="x-p"/> And under Tyrian robes the lamb shall bleat." <div eID="gen3611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3612" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen3612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3613" type="x-p"/> Badgers' skins - ערת תחשים oroth techashim. Few terms have afforded greater perplexity to critics and commentators than this. Bochart has exhausted the subject, and seems to have proved that no kind of animal is here intended, but a color. None of the ancient versions acknowledge an animal of any kind except the Chaldee, which seems to think the badger is intended, and from it we have borrowed our translation of the word. The Septuagint and Vulgate have skins dyed a violet color; the Syriac, azure; the Arabic, black; the Coptic, violet; the modern Persic, ram-skins, etc. The color contended for by Bochart is the hysginus, which is a very deep blue. So Pliny, Coccoque tinctum Tyrio tingere, ut fieret hysginum. "They dip crimson in purple to make the color called hysginus." - Hist. Nat., lib. ix., c. 65, edit. Bipont. <div eID="gen3613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3614" type="x-p"/> Shittim wood - By some supposed to be the finest species of the cedar; by others, the acacia Nilotica, a species of thorn, solid, light, and very beautiful. This acacia is known to have been plentiful in Egypt, and it abounds in Arabia Deserta, the very place in which Moses was when he built the tabernacle; and hence it is reasonable to suppose that he built it of that wood, which was every way proper for his purpose.
entries.2da1ac880e8ed43a3a9fc3d67102b38abce7f1d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen3614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3615" type="x-p"/> Oil for the light - This they must have brought with them from Egypt, for they could not get any in the wilderness where there were no olives; but it is likely that this and some other directions refer more to what was to be done when in their fixed and settled residence, than while wandering in the wilderness. <div eID="gen3615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3616" type="x-p"/> Spices - To make a confection for sweet incense, abounded in different parts of these countries.
entries.4667c387c6f21866d9685eba088cd093bbf1b61f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen3616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3617" type="x-p"/> Onyx stones - We have already met with the stone called שהם shoham, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.12">Gen 2:12</reference>, and acknowledged the difficulty of ascertaining what is meant by it. Some think the onyx, some the sardine, and some the emerald, is meant. We cannot say precisely what it was; possibly it might have been that fine pale pebble, called the Egyptian pebble, several specimens of which now lie before me, which were brought from the coast of the Red Sea, and other parts in Egypt, by a particular friend of mine, on purpose to add to my collection of minerals. Stones to be set in the ephod - אבני מלאים abney milluim, stones of filling up. Stones so cut as to be proper to be set in the gold work of the breastplate. <div eID="gen3617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3618" type="x-p"/> The אפד ephod - It is very difficult to tell what this was, or in what form it was made. It was a garment of some kind peculiar to the priests, and ever considered essential to all the parts of Divine worship, for without it no person attempted to inquire of God. As the word itself comes from the root אפד aphad, he tied or bound close, Calmet supposes that it was a kind of girdle, which, brought from behind the neck and over the shoulders, and so hanging down before, was put cross upon the stomach, and then carried round the waist, and thus made a girdle to the tunic. Where the ephod crossed on the breast there was a square ornament called חשן choshen, the breastplate, in which twelve precious stones were set, each bearing one of the names of the twelve sons of Jacob engraven on it. There were two sorts of ephods, one of plain linen for the priests, the other very much embroidered for the high priest. As there was nothing singular in this common sort, no particular description is given; but that of the high priest is described very much in detail <reference osisRef="Exo.28.6-Exo.28.8">Exo 28:6-8</reference>. It was distinguished from the common ephod by being composed of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, fine twisted linen, and cunning work, i.e., superbly ornamented and embroidered. This ephod was fastened on the shoulders with two precious stones, on which the twelve names of the twelve tribes of Israel were engraved, six names on each stone. These two stones, thus engraved, were different from those on the breastplate, with which they have been confounded. From Calmet's description the ephod seems to have been a series of belts, fastened to a collar, which were intended to keep the garments of the priest closely attached to his body: but there is some reason to believe that it was a sort of garment like that worn by our heralds; it covered the back, breast, and belly, and was open at the sides. A piece of the same kind of stuff with itself united it on the shoulders, where the two stones, already mentioned, were placed, and it was probably without sleeves. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.2">Exo 28:2</reference> (note), etc.
entries.f174013caf91096817dc401361bf3c98e299b89c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen3618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3619" type="x-p"/> Let them make me a sanctuary - מקדש mikdash, a holy place, such as God might dwell in; this was that part of the tabernacle that was called the most holy place, into which the high priest entered only once a year, on the great day of atonement. <div eID="gen3619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3620" type="x-p"/> That I may dwell among them - "This," says Mr. Ainsworth, "was the main end of all; and to this all the particulars are to be referred, and by this they are to be opened. For this sanctuary, as Solomon's temple afterwards, was the place of prayer, and of the public service of God, <reference osisRef="Lev.17.4-Lev.17.6">Lev 17:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.21.13">Mat 21:13</reference>; and it signified the Church which is the habitation of God through the Spirit, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Cor 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19-Eph.2.22">Eph 2:19-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Rev 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev 21:3</reference>; and was a visible sign of God's presence and protection, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Lev 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">Lev 26:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.37.27">Eze 37:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.37.28">Eze 37:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.12">1Kgs 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.13">1Kgs 6:13</reference>; and of his leading them to his heavenly glory. For as the high priest entered into the tabernacle, and through the veil into the most holy place where God dwelt; so Christ entered into the holy of holies, and we also enter through the veil, that is to say his flesh. See the use made of this by the apostle, Hebrews 9 and 10. Thus the sanctuary is to be applied as a type, <div eID="gen3620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3621" type="x-p"/> 1. To Christ's person, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">Heb 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">Heb 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.2.19-Joh.2.21">Joh 2:19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen3621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3622" type="x-p"/> 2. To every Christian, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">1Cor 6:19</reference>. <div eID="gen3622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3623" type="x-p"/> 3. To the Church; both particular, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">Heb 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Tim 3:15</reference>; and universal, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.21">Heb 10:21</reference> : and it was because of the very extensive signification of this building, that the different things concerning this sanctuary are particularly set down by Moses, and so variously applied by the prophets and by the apostles." - See Ainsworth. <div eID="gen3623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3624" type="x-p"/> As the dwelling in this tabernacle was the highest proof of God's grace and mercy towards the Israelites, so it typified Christ's dwelling by faith in the hearts of believers, and thus giving them the highest and surest proof of their reconciliation to God, and of his love and favor to them; see <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Eph 1:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Eph 3:17</reference>.
entries.324b6f64ff2dbf976dedc666c5b88bcf151bf1ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen3624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3625" type="x-p"/> After the pattern of the tabernacle - It has been supposed that there had been a tabernacle before that erected by Moses, though it probably did not now exist; but the tabernacle which Moses is ordered to make was to be formed exactly on the model of this ancient one, the pattern of which God showed him in the mount, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.40">Exo 25:40</reference>. The word משכן mishcan signifies literally the dwelling or habitation; and this was so called because it was the dwelling place of God; and the only place on the earth in which he made himself manifest. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.40">Exo 25:40</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Exo.33.7-Exo.33.10">Exo 33:7-10</reference>.
entries.88c43089d8e028fbc80a51854e7c2f8020ed45ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen3625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3626" type="x-p"/> They shall make an ark - ארון aron signifies an ark, chest, coffer, or coffin. It is used particularly to designate that chest or coffer in which the testimony or two tables of the covenant was laid up, on the top of which was the propitiatory or mercy-seat, (see on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.17">Exo 25:17</reference>), and at the end of which were the cherubim of gold, (<reference osisRef="Exo.25.18-Exo.25.20">Exo 25:18-20</reference>), between whom the visible sign of the presence of the supreme God appeared as seated upon his throne. The ark was the most excellent of all the holy things which belonged to the Mosaic economy, and for its sake the tabernacle and the temple were built, <reference osisRef="Exo.26.33">Exo 26:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.40.18">Exo 40:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.40.21">Exo 40:21</reference>. It was considered as conferring a sanctity wherever it was fixed, 2 Chronicles 8;11; <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.12">2Sam 6:12</reference>. <div eID="gen3626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3627" type="x-p"/> Two cubits and a half shall be the length, etc. - About four feet five inches in length, taking the cubit as twenty-one inches, and two feet six inches in breadth and in depth. As this ark was chiefly intended to deposit the two tables of stone in, which had been written by the finger of God, we may very reasonably conjecture that the length of those tables was not less than four feet and their breadth not less than two. As to their thickness we can say nothing, as the depth of the ark was intended for other matters besides the two tables, such as Aaron's rod, the pot of manna, etc., etc., though probably these were laid up beside, not in, the ark.
entries.bd75fead3803c1d7f3be338400549c992ad1dee7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen3627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3628" type="x-p"/> A crown of gold round about - A border, or, as the Septuagint have it, κυματια χρυσα στεπτα κυκλω, waves of gold wreathed round about.
entries.aba1ca3a0f6f1de282de09544e807d7565b0e29b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen3628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3629" type="x-p"/> The staves - shall not be taken from it - Because it should ever be considered as in readiness to be removed, God not having told them at what hour he should command them to strike their tents. If the staves were never to be taken out, how can it be said, as in <reference osisRef="Num.4.6">Num 4:6</reference>, that when the camp should set forward, they should put in the staves thereof, which intimates that when they encamped, they took out the staves, which appears to be contrary to what is here said? To reconcile these two places, it has been supposed, with great show of probability, that besides the staves which passed through the rings of the ark, and by which it was carried, there were two other staves or poles in the form of a bier or handbarrow, on which the ark was laid in order to be transported in their journeyings, when it and its own staves, still in their rings, had been wrapped up in the covering of what is called badgers' skins and blue cloth. The staves of the ark itself, which might be considered as its handles simply to lift it by, were never taken out of their rings; but the staves or poles which served as a bier were taken from under it when they encamped.
entries.5fed06221b67906c5f7b7238050096519d6d6f8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen3629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3630" type="x-p"/> The testimony - The two tables of stone which were not yet given; these tables were called עדת eduth, from עד forward, onward, to bear witness to or of a person or thing. Not only the tables of stone, but all the contents of the ark, Aaron's rod, the pot of manna, the holy anointing oil, etc., bore testimony to the Messiah in his prophetic, sacerdotal, and regal offices.
entries.9f5b2ef0467d212c92459afcfa9ceafef3981216: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen3630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3631" type="x-p"/> A mercy-seat - כפרת capporeth, from כפר caphar, to cover or overspread; because by an act of pardon sins are represented as being covered, so that they no longer appear in the eye of Divine justice to displease, irritate, and call for punishment; and the person of the offender is covered or protected from the stroke of the broken law. In the Greek version of the Septuagint the word ιλαστηριον, hilasterion, is used, which signifies a propitiatory, and is the name used by the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.5">Heb 9:5</reference>. This mercy-seat or propitiatory was made of pure gold; it was properly the lid or covering of that vessel so well known by the name of the ark and ark of the covenant. On and before this, the high priest was to sprinkle the blood of the expiatory sacrifices on the great day of atonement: and it was in this place that God promised to meet the people, (see <reference osisRef="Exo.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>); for there he dwelt, and there was the symbol of the Divine presence. At each end of this propitiatory was a cherub, between whom this glory was manifested; hence in Scripture it is so often said that he dwelleth between the cherubim. As the word ιλαστηριον, propitiatory or mercy-seat, is applied to Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Rom 3:25</reference>, whom God hath set forth to be a Propitiation (ιλαστηριον) through faith in his blood - for the remission of sins that are past; hence we learn that Christ was the true mercy-seat, the thing signified by the capporeth, to the ancient believers. And we learn farther that it was by his blood that an atonement was to be made for the sins of the world. And as God showed himself between the cherubim over this propitiatory or mercy-seat, so it is said, God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Cor 5:19</reference>, etc. See on Leviticus 7 (note).
entries.7c6aad7634f50e701691235b14968d3e191e9593: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen3631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3632" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt make two cherubims - What these were we cannot distinctly say. It is generally supposed that a cherub was a creature with four heads and one body: and the animals, of which these emblematical forms consisted, were the noblest of their kinds; the lion among the wild beasts, the bull among the tame ones, the eagle among the birds, and man at the head of all; so that they might be, says Dr. Priestley, the representatives of all nature. Concerning their forms and design there is much difference of opinion among divines. It is probable that the term often means a figure of any kind, such as was ordinarily sculptured on stone, engraved on metal, carved on wood, or embroidered on cloth. See on <reference osisRef="Exo.35.8">Exo 35:8</reference> (note). It may be only necessary to add, that cherub is the singular number; cherubim, not cherubims, the plural. See what has been said on this subject in the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen 3:24</reference> (note).
entries.f2a3ba564488559f84e74c7f175cc50299c1140e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen3632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3633" type="x-p"/> And there I will meet with thee - That is, over the mercy-seat, between the cherubim. In this place God chose to give the most especial manifestations of himself; here the Divine glory was to be seen; and here Moses was to come in order to consult Jehovah, relative to the management of the people. <div eID="gen3633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3634" type="x-p"/> Ainsworth has remarked that the rabbins say, "The heart of man may be likened to God's sanctuary; for as, in the sanctuary, the shechinah or Divine glory dwelt, because there were the ark, the tables, and the cherubim; so, in the heart of man, it is meet that a place be made for the Divine Majesty to dwell in, and that it be the holy of holies." This is a doctrine most implicitly taught by the apostles; and the absolute necessity of having the heart made a habitation of God through the Spirit, is strongly and frequently insisted on through the whole of the New Testament. See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.23">Exo 25:23</reference>.
entries.86fde6f7763aa813c8cf5780ab0393e316cf5a4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen3634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3635" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt also make a table of shittim wood - The same wood, the acacia, of which the arkstaves, etc., were made. On the subject of the ark, table of shew-bread, etc., Dr. Cudworth, in his very learned and excellent treatise on the Lord's Supper, has the following remarks: - "When God had brought the children of Israel out of Egypt, resolving to manifest himself in a peculiar manner present among them, he thought good to dwell amongst them in a visible and external manner; and therefore, while they were in the wilderness, and sojourned in tents, he would have a tent or tabernacle built to sojourn with them also. This mystery of the tabernacle was fully understood by the learned Nachmanides, who, in few words, but pregnant, expresseth himself to this purpose: 'The mystery of the tabernacle was this, that it was to be a place for the shechinah, or habitation of Divinity, to be fixed in;' and this, no doubt, as a special type of God's future dwelling in Christ's human nature, which was the True Shechinah: but when the Jews were come into their land, and had there built them houses, God intended to have a fixed dwelling-house also; and therefore his movable tabernacle was to be turned into a standing temple. Now the tabernacle or temple, being thus as a house for God to dwell in visibly, to make up the notion of dwelling or habitation complete there must be all things suitable to a house belonging to it; hence, in the holy place, there must be a table, and a candlestick, because this was the ordinary furniture of a room, as the fore-commended Nachmanides observes. The table must have its dishes, and spoons, and bowls, and covers belonging to it, though they were never used; and always be furnished with bread upon it. The candlestick must have its lamps continually burning. Hence also there must be a continual fire kept in this house of God upon the altar, as the focus of it; to which notion I conceive the Prophet Isaiah doth allude, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference> : Whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem; and besides all this, to carry the notion still farther, there must be some constant meat and provision brought into this house; which was done in the sacrifices that were partly consumed by fire upon God's own altar, and partly eaten by the priests, who were God's family, and therefore to be maintained by him. That which was consumed upon God's altar was accounted God's mess, as appeareth from <reference osisRef="Mal.1.12">Mal 1:12</reference>, where the altar is called God's table, and the sacrifice upon it, God's meat: Ye say, The table of the Lord is polluted; and the fruit thereof, even His Meat, is contemptible. And often, in the law, the sacrifice is called God's לחם lechem, i.e., his bread or food. Wherefore it is farther observable, that besides the flesh of the beast offered up in sacrifice, there was a minchah, i.e., a meat-offering, or rather bread-offering, made of flour and oil; and a libamen or drink-offering, which was always joined with the daily sacrifice, as the bread and drink which was to go along with God's meat.
